usamts-2017-r1-01.title: Walk through the cube of numbers
usamts-2017-r1-01.body:
Think of each number $abc$ as a point of a $3\times3\times3$ cube; neighbouring squares must hold points that differ in exactly one coordinate (in either direction, e.g. $212$ next to $232$ or $222$ or $211$ ...). Each white square's neighbours must therefore lie on one of the three lines through it.

A square between two givens is especially constrained: e.g. the white square in row 3, column 6 touches $113$ below it and $131$ to its right, so it must differ from each of them in exactly one digit: only $111$ and $133$ qualify. Working outward from the givens in this way, and using that each of the 27 numbers occurs only once, leads to
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline  &  &  & 233 & 232 & 212 & 222 & 122\\\hline 231 & \blacksquare & 223 & 213 & \blacksquare & 112 & \blacksquare & 123\\\hline 331 & \blacksquare & 221 & 211 & 311 & 111 & 131 & 133\\\hline 332 & \blacksquare & 121 & \blacksquare & 313 & 113 & \blacksquare & 132\\\hline 333 & 323 & 321 & 322 & 312 &  &  & \\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** All 27 numbers $111, \dots, 333$ appear exactly once, and every pair of side-adjacent white squares differs in exactly one digit, for example row 1: $233 \to 232 \to 212 \to 222 \to 122$ (each step changes one digit), and column 1: $231 \to 331 \to 332 \to 333$. A computer search confirms that this is the only solution.

**Answer: the grid above.**

usamts-2017-r1-02.title: Write the condition and watch $k$ cancel
usamts-2017-r1-02.body:
Suppose Noah's rating was $r$ (with $1 < r < 5$) after $k$ rides, so his ratings so far add up to $kr$. After the 1-star ride and $n$ further 5-star rides, his average is
$$\frac{kr + 1 + 5n}{k + 1 + n}.$$
This is at least $r$ exactly when
$$kr + 1 + 5n \ge kr + r + rn \iff 1 + 5n \ge r(n + 1) \iff n(5 - r) \ge r - 1 \iff n \ge \frac{r-1}{5-r}$$
(dividing by $5 - r > 0$). The $kr$ terms cancelled, so the condition does not depend on $k$. The number of 5-star ratings he needs is the least integer $n$ satisfying it,
$$n = \left\lceil \frac{r-1}{5-r} \right\rceil,$$
which depends only on $r$, not on the number of rides. (Intuitively: the old rides have average exactly $r$, so the new block of rides — one 1 and $n$ fives — must itself average at least $r$.) ∎

usamts-2017-r1-03.title: A 30-60-90 triangle cut in two
usamts-2017-r1-03.body:
**The pieces.** Let $A = (0,0)$, $C = (\sqrt3, 0)$, $B = (\sqrt3, 1)$: a right triangle with right angle at $C$, $\angle A = 30^\circ$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and hypotenuse $AB = 2$. Let $P = \left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \frac12\right)$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and let the perpendicular to $AB$ at $P$ meet $AC$ at $Q = \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}, 0\right)$. This cuts $ABC$ into
* the **triangle** $T = APQ$: angles $30^\circ$ at $A$, $90^\circ$ at $P$, $60^\circ$ at $Q$; sides $AP = 1$, $PQ = \frac1{\sqrt3}$, $AQ = \frac2{\sqrt3}$;
* the **quadrilateral** $K = QCBP$: angles $120^\circ$ at $Q$, $90^\circ$ at $C$, $60^\circ$ at $B$, $90^\circ$ at $P$; sides $QC = \sqrt3 - \frac2{\sqrt3} = \frac1{\sqrt3}$, $CB = 1$, $BP = 1$, $PQ = \frac1{\sqrt3}$.

**1. Triangle:** $T \cup K = ABC$.

**2. Convex quadrilateral:** rotate $T$ by $180^\circ$ about $P$. Since $P$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $A$ goes to $B$, and $Q$ goes to $Q' = 2P - Q$ on the other side of line $AB$, so the rotated triangle $BPQ'$ lies outside $K$ and shares the side $BP$ with it. The union has vertices $Q', B, C, Q$: at $P$ the angles $90^\circ + 90^\circ$ make a straight line $Q'PQ$, at $B$ we get $30^\circ + 60^\circ = 90^\circ$, and the other angles are $90^\circ$ at $C$, $120^\circ$ at $Q$, $60^\circ$ at $Q'$. All are below $180^\circ$: a convex quadrilateral.

**3. Convex pentagon:** move $T$ (by a rotation and translation) so that its leg $AP$ of length 1 lies along the side $CB$ of length 1, with $A \to C$, $P \to B$, and $Q \to Q'' = \left(\sqrt3 + \frac1{\sqrt3}, 1\right)$ on the outer side of $CB$. (This preserves orientation: both $A, P, Q$ and $C, B, Q''$ are clockwise, so no reflection is used.) The union has vertices $Q, C, Q'', B, P$ with angles $120^\circ$ at $Q$, $90^\circ + 30^\circ = 120^\circ$ at $C$, $60^\circ$ at $Q''$, $60^\circ + 90^\circ = 150^\circ$ at $B$, and $90^\circ$ at $P$. These sum to $540^\circ$ and are all less than $180^\circ$: a convex pentagon.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

usamts-2017-r1-04.title: Give the opponent the smallest numbers
usamts-2017-r1-04.body:
**Key fact.** A row containing both 1 and 2 loses: its product is at most $1\cdot2\cdot7\cdot8 = 112$, while the other row then has four numbers from $\{3, \dots, 8\}$, with product at least $3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6 = 360$.

**Strategy for the first player.**
1. First move: place 1 in the bottom row.
2. If the second player does anything other than placing 2 in the top row, the 2 is still available and the bottom row still has room, so the first player places 2 in the bottom row; the bottom row now contains 1 and 2 and loses by the key fact.
3. So the second player places 2 in the top row. The first player now places 3 in the bottom row.

Now the bottom row contains 1 and 3, so its final product is at most $1\cdot3\cdot7\cdot8 = 168$. The top row contains 2 and three numbers from $\{4, \dots, 8\}$, so its product is at least $2\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6 = 240 > 168$. Whatever happens afterwards, the top product is larger.

(A computer search of the whole game tree confirms that the first player wins.)

**Answer: the first player wins.** ∎

usamts-2017-r1-05.title: Decimal tags
usamts-2017-r1-05.body:
**Construction.** Enumerate all integers as $s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots$ (e.g. $0, 1, -1, 2, -2, \dots$). Let $r_k = \sum_{i=1}^k 10^{-i} = 0.\underbrace{11\ldots1}_{k}$ and
$$S = \{-10^{-k} : k \ge 1\} \cup \{t_k = s_k + r_k : k \ge 1\}.$$
(These are all distinct rationals: the $t_k$ have fractional parts $r_k$, all different, while $-10^{-j}$ has fractional part $0.99\ldots9 \ne r_k$.)

**Existence.** For the integer $n = s_k$: $t_k - 10^{-1} - 10^{-2} - \dots - 10^{-k} = s_k$.

**Uniqueness.** Take any nonempty finite subset, with $T$ the set of indices of the $t_k$'s used and $U$ the set of $j$ with $-10^{-j}$ used. Its sum is $\sum_{k\in T} s_k + X$ where
$$X = \sum_{k \in T} r_k - \sum_{j\in U} 10^{-j} = \sum_{i \ge 1} e_i\, 10^{-i},\qquad e_i = c_i - u_i,$$
with $c_i = \#\{k \in T: k \ge i\}$ (how many chosen $r_k$ have a 1 in decimal place $i$) and $u_i = 1$ if $i \in U$, else $0$. The sum is an integer iff $X$ is.

*Claim: if $X$ is an integer then all $e_i = 0$.* Otherwise let $L$ be the largest index with $e_L \ne 0$. Then $10^L X \equiv e_L \pmod{10}$, so $10 \mid e_L$. Let $K = \max T$ (if $T$ is empty, $e_L = -1$, impossible). If $L > K$ then $c_L = 0$ and $e_L = -u_L = -1$; if $L = K$ then $c_L = 1$ and $e_L \in \{0, 1\}$; if $L < K$ then $e_i = 0$ for $L < i \le K$, so $c_i = u_i \le 1$, while $c_i \ge 1$; thus $c_{L+1} = 1$ and $c_L \le c_{L+1} + 1 = 2$, so $|e_L| \le 2$. In every case $e_L$ is a nonzero number of absolute value at most 2, not divisible by 10. Contradiction.

So $e_i = 0$ for all $i$, i.e. $c_i = u_i \le 1$. Then $c_1 = |T| \le 1$; $T$ empty would force $U$ empty (all $u_i = c_i = 0$), but the subset is nonempty. Hence $T = \{k\}$, $c_i = 1$ exactly for $i \le k$, so $U = \{1, \dots, k\}$, and the sum is $s_k$. As each integer appears exactly once as some $s_k$, every integer $n$ has exactly one representation. ∎

**Answer: Yes.**
